How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

:::

Full text

Abstract

This exploratory study examines how gender and personality relate in natural language expression, illustrating how Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques can be used in psychological research. By analyzing stream-of-consciousness essays from 2,240 undergraduates using BERT with integrated gradients attribution, we identify words and texts that the model relies on to distinguish men's from women's writing, and examine whether they differ across trait levels. Our approach illustrates how explainability methods can help surface candidate patterns in language use across trait levels and between males and females. Logistic regression predicting gender from self-reported Big Five scores reveals Neuroticism as the strongest predictor (OR = 2.11, p ≤ .001), followed by Extraversion and Agreeableness. The BERT model achieves a balanced accuracy of 0.815 in gender classification. Reading the texts with the highest attribution scores, gender-typical content (e.g., romantic relationships, social affiliation) dominated at both low and high trait levels, alongside a few tentative trait-specific patterns that we offer as hypotheses for future work. These findings suggest that attribution-guided reading of texts can generate interpretable, testable hypotheses about trait-level patterns in language, complementing traditional methods.

Introduction

Gender Differences in Personality and Their Expression in Language

Whether and how men and women differ psychologically remains a question of substantial interest in personality science (Rauthmann & Kuper, 2025). Meta-analyses have documented gender differences ranging from assertiveness and anxiety (Else-Quest et al., 2006; Feingold, 1994) to the Big Five domains, on which women score higher on average in Neuroticism, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Extraversion (except for its assertiveness facet), and men in Openness, specifically to Ideas (Costa et al., 2001; Kajonius & Johnson, 2018; Lippa, 2010; Vianello et al., 2013). These differences appear across cultures, although the claim that they are larger in more gender-egalitarian countries (Costa et al., 2001; Lippa, 2010; Schmitt et al., 2008) has been challenged by a recent reanalysis, in which the association was attenuated, and sometimes non-significant or even reversed, once cultural region and data quality were taken into account (Berggren & Bergh, 2025). Most of this evidence also rests on global self-reports, which may reflect gender stereotypes and identity as well as how people think, feel, and behave. In an experience-sampling study, gender differences in emotional stability, agreeableness, and conscientiousness were larger in global trait reports than in average momentary states, where they were not significant, although equivalence could not be established (Buck et al., 2026).

One way to look beyond global self-reports is to examine how traits are expressed. Language is particularly suited to this, because it is both a behavior and an expression of thoughts and feelings that reveals important aspects of individuals' social and psychological worlds (Pennebaker et al., 2003). It has been used to study personality (Park et al., 2014; Schwartz et al., 2013; Tackman et al., 2020) and gender: in a large LIWC-based analysis, women used more words related to social and psychological processes, and men more words referring to objects and impersonal topics (Newman et al., 2008), and metaanalytic evidence shows gender differences in several aspects of language use (Leaper & Ayres, 2007). Far fewer studies have examined how gender and personality jointly relate to language use, and their results disagree (see Table 1 1 ). Mehl et al. (2006) used Electronically Activated Recorders (EAR) to sample spontaneous spoken language in daily life and found significant differences between men and women in how personality traits showed up in behavior. A later study with a larger and more diverse sample (462 compared to the original 96 participants) found few such differences: only 5% of trait-behavior correlations (31 of 620) differed significantly between men and women (Tackman et al., 2020). Estimates are imprecise even for a simpler measure: in a preregistered replication of Mehl et al. (2007) pooling 22 samples (N = 2,197), Tidwell et al. (2025) found a small gender difference in the number of words spoken per day (d = 0.13), but the estimate was too imprecise to establish either equivalence or a meaningful difference.

Why Trait Levels Matter

Part of this disagreement may arise because gender differences in language are not consistent across trait levels: individuals with low or high trait scores might show different patterns from those at moderate levels (Hofmann et al., 2025; Tackman et al., 2020). For instance, women typically score higher on Neuroticism than men, yet Tackman et al. (2020) found that higher Neuroticism was associated with more sadness-related words among women but not among men. Two complementary theoretical frameworks motivate examining such variation.

First, Whole Trait Theory (WTT) proposes that personality traits are density distributions of states rather than fixed characteristics, with the expression of traits varying across moments and contexts through social-cognitive mechanisms (Fleeson & Jayawickreme, 2015). WTT was developed to account for within-person situational variability, but its central insight, that identical trait levels can produce different behavioral expressions depending on individual characteristics, can be extended to stable characteristics such as gender. Men and women with similar trait levels may then enact those traits differently in language.

Second, research on person-situation interactions has documented individual differences in how people respond to situational characteristics, and these contingencies between situation characteristics and personality states are themselves important individual difference variables (Kuper et al., 2022 (Kuper et al., , 2024)). People also perceive identical situations differently, and this idiosyncratic variance depends on characteristics such as personality traits and demographic factors, including gender (Horstmann et al., 2021). Extending this framework to verbal expression, gender differences in language use may vary systematically across personality trait levels.

From Word Counts to Explainable Models

Studying such variation requires methods that can capture it. Language analysis in psychology has moved from word counting toward context-sensitive representations (Boyd & Schwartz, 2021). Closed-vocabulary methods such as the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) count words in predefined categories, whereas open-vocabulary methods such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) derive categories from the texts themselves (Eichstaedt et al., 2021; Park et al., 2014). Both have yielded many findings into personality and gender (Park et al., 2014 (Park et al., , 2016;; Schwartz et al., 2013; Tackman et al., 2020), but both treat words or topics as isolated units: a dictionary counts "bank" identically whether it refers to a financial institution or a riverbank. They may therefore miss subtler differences in how men and women express the same trait.

Transformer models such as BERT (Rogers et al., 2020; Vaswani et al., 2017) build contextualized representations, in which the same word is represented differently depending on its surroundings (see Materials and Methods). In psychology, they have been used to improve the prediction of personality traits and to revisit aspects of the lexical hypothesis (Saeteros et al., 2025) (Cutler & Condon, 2022).

These capabilities do not replace psychological theory, which is still needed to interpret what the models detect. Models used only to maximize prediction accuracy can show that language carries trait-related signal, but not why, or for whom. Moving from prediction toward understanding requires interpreting model outputs within personality theory and considering how verbal expression interacts with situational contexts (e.g., assessment settings, communication media) and with other psychological variables, such as gender (Boyd & Markowitz, 2024). Such integration could also help the field build explanatory accounts of trait expression on a descriptive foundation (Boyd & Pennebaker, 2017).

XAI offers a practical route toward this integration. By identifying which linguistic features contribute most to a model's predictions, it shows how patterns vary across trait levels or between groups, and links trait scores to specific words and texts. This contribution is, at first, descriptive: it specifies which words co-occur with which trait levels, in which gender, and in which contexts. Such descriptive findings are the material from which explanatory accounts can later be built (Mõttus et al., 2020), because they define what theories of trait expression must account for. To our knowledge, contextual models with XAI have not yet been used to study how gender differences in language vary across trait levels.

Present Study

We adopt an exploratory, hypothesis-generating design, following the approach of (Saeteros et al., 2025): a BERT classifier trained to distinguish men's from women's essays, whose predictions are inspected with integrated gradients. Integrated gradients show which words drive each prediction, so that the detected patterns can be read and interpreted, following an approach recently discussed for psychology in the context of correlations (Mõttus, 2022). We intend it as a step toward explanatory accounts, generating specific, testable patterns that later work can examine with designs capable of addressing mechanisms, such as prompted-topic writing tasks, experience sampling combined with language data (Buck et al., 2026), or preregistered confirmatory tests on independent corpora.

Research Questions and Objectives

We ask (1) how men's and women's language use differs overall, and (2) how it differs between men and women who share similar trait levels, with particular attention to the lowest and highest quartiles of each trait.

Materials and Methods

Analysis Overview

Our study followed a workflow similar to that of Saeteros et al. (2025), organized in three phases (Figure 1). In Phase 1, the essays were split into fragments and the personality scores were standardized. In Phase 2, we conducted two preliminary analyses of the personality scores and two language analyses: the log-odds ratio with Informative Dirichlet Prior (IDP), and the attribution of the predictions of a BERT gender classifier using integrated gradients. In Phase 3, the outputs of the language analyses were used to identify and interpret the linguistic patterns that characterize each gender.

Both language analyses were conducted under two aspects. The Gender Only aspect examined gender differences in language use regardless of personality, whereas the Gender and Personality aspect compared males and females within extreme trait groups (e.g., females with high Agreeableness scores vs. males with high Agreeableness scores), following an approach similar to that of Mõttus (2022) but using quartiles instead of tertiles. Quartiles were computed on the year-standardized z-scores of each trait: low trait groups (Q1) comprised participants at or below the 25th percentile and high trait groups (Q4) those above the 75th percentile. For the log-odds analysis, cut-offs were computed on the whole sample, so that men and women in each group had the same absolute trait level; for the attribution analysis, they were computed separately for males and females, so that each gender contributed a comparable number of texts to the selection of high-attribution words.

The classifier was trained to predict gender, not personality. Its attribution scores therefore identify what distinguishes men's from women's writing, and trait information enters only through the stratification of participants into low and high trait groups. We do not infer personality traits from vocabulary.

Phase 1: Dataset and Preprocessing

We used the Essays dataset (Pennebaker & King, 1999), which contains 2,240 streamof-consciousness essays (1,342 females and 898 males) written freely for 20 minutes by undergraduate students between 1997 and 2004foot_1 . We chose it for two reasons. First, the essays were written in response to a minimal, open-ended instruction: participants were asked to write about their thoughts, feelings, and sensations at that moment, as they came to them, continuously and without concern for grammar, sentence structure, or spelling (Pennebaker & King, 1999). Topic and style were therefore not imposed by a platform or an audience, and the texts may reflect thoughts and feelings more than conversational behavior shaped by an interlocutor or setting. Second, every participant also completed a 44-item Big Five Inventory (John et al., 1991) in a version with simplified item wording, and the corpus is, to our knowledge, one of the most widely studied datasets pairing free text with Big Five scores (Mairesse et al., 2007), which allows our results to be compared with a large body of prior work. Its main limitations are its age and the assigned academic writing context (see Limitations). Other corpora with Big Five scores exist: myPersonality, built on Facebook, is no longer available (Stillwell & Kosinski, 2015), and PANDORA, built on Reddit (Gjurković et al., 2021), is left for future work.

Because our dataset's "sex" variable was self-reported, we interpret it as reflecting gender identity rather than biological sex (American Psychological Association, 2020, Section 5.5) and use the term gender throughout, while acknowledging that the dataset does not capture gender beyond this binary classification. Likewise, "trait" and "trait level" refer throughout to scores on the self-report Big Five inventory, not to an underlying disposition.

Since the inventory was scored differently across years (sum scores in some years, mean scores in others), personality scores were standardized within each year using z-scores. Because the essays exceeded BERT's 512-token limit, they were divided into 256-word fragments, each of which inherited the gender label of its essay.

Phase 2: Personality and Language Analyses

Gender Differences in Personality Traits

As a preliminary validation step, we computed Cohen's d effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for each trait and fitted a logistic regression predicting gender from the five traits. These analyses check that the sample reproduces the gender differences in personality reported in previous research before we turn to language.

Log-odds Ratio with Informative Dirichlet Prior

The log-odds ratio with IDP (Monroe et al., 2008) identifies words whose usage frequency differs between groups. It compares the odds of each word in the two groups, which accounts for differences in corpus size, and uses an informative Dirichlet prior given by the combined word counts of the two groups being compared, which shrinks estimates for rare words toward their overall frequency. The resulting z-scores are positive for greater female usage and negative for greater male usage. Two-sided p-values were adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) over the vocabulary of each comparison, with q < .05 as the significance criterion. We computed z-scores for the whole sample (Gender Only aspect) and within the Q1 and Q4 groups of each trait (Gender and Personality aspect). In addition, a two-proportion z-test compared the proportion of males using "girlfriend" with the proportion of females using "boyfriend".

Gender Classification and Feature Attribution

We fine-tuned BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), a language model based on the transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). Transformers are neural networks built around an attention mechanism, which allows the model to weigh, for each word, how relevant every other word in the text is to its interpretation. BERT was pre-trained on large text corpora. Pre-training provides the model with general knowledge of language structure and meaning, which fine-tuning then adapts to a specific task with far less labelled data than training from scratch. BERT splits text into subword tokens and, by stacking several attention layers, builds a representation of each token that takes into account both its left and right context. As a result, unlike word-counting approaches, the same word can contribute differently to a prediction depending on how it is used. In this study, BERT was fine-tuned to predict the author's gender from each fragment. Performance was evaluated at the fragment level with the balanced accuracy (the mean of sensitivity and specificity, robust to class imbalance). The fragments were randomly partitioned into training (90%) and test (10%) sets, and 10% of the training set was held out as a validation set to select the best training epoch (see Implementation Details).

To identify the words driving the model's predictions, we applied integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al., 2017) to the test set fragments. This method integrates the model's gradients along a path from a baseline input to the actual input, assigning each token a score that indicates whether it increased (positive score) or decreased (negative score) the probability of the predicted class. Token scores are summed to obtain a text-level score for the whole fragment. Since attributions are assigned to the subword tokens of the BERT tokenizer, each token was treated as a unit of analysis, which we refer to as a word for simplicity.

Following Saeteros et al. (2025), within the fragments predicted as each gender, we separated positive attributions (supporting the predicted class) from negative attributions (supporting the opposite class), so that, for instance, a negative attribution in a fragment predicted as female was taken as evidence for the male class. We then applied the maximum attribution technique, which keeps the highest absolute score of each word across all its occurrences, and visualized these scores with bar plots and word clouds (Halvey & Keane, 2007). Only correctly classified fragments, and words appearing at least 10 times in them, were considered. The same model was used for both aspects: attributions for the Gender and Personality aspect were obtained by filtering the test fragments by gender and trait quartile.

Two additional checks addressed potential shortcuts in the model. First, to assess the influence of obvious gender-identifying terms, we trained the model on a version of the data in which relationship terms ("boyfriend", "girlfriend", and their variants) were masked. Second, because our aim was to characterize gender-linked language rather than to build a classifier, the data were split at the fragment level, so that the full content of every essay contributed to the analysis; consequently, fragments from the same essay may appear in different partitions, which could lead the model to rely on author-specific cues. However, the top-ranked attribution words (Figure 3) were not author-specific: each appeared in at least 45 different essays, and no single essay accounted for more than 8% of its occurrences. Moreover, with an author-level split, balanced accuracy decreased only slightly (0.797 vs. 0.815), as expected given the small number of fragments per essay (median = 3).

Phase 3: Selection and Interpretation of Attribution Outputs

In Phase 3, the log-odds z-scores identified words with greater female or male usage, either in the whole sample or within each trait quartile. The attribution scores were used to select the fragments to be examined, so that selection relied on the model rather than on researcher choice. For each gender, we took the five words with the highest maximum attribution scores and, for each of them, examined the 10 fragments in which the word reached its highest attribution score and the 10 fragments containing the word with the highest text-level attribution scores. In the Gender Only aspect, we additionally examined, for each gender, the 10 fragments with the highest text-level attribution scores. The Gender and Personality aspect applied the same word-level procedure within each combination of gender, trait, and quartile (e.g., female-Q1-Agreeableness).

Interpretation followed two steps. First, the selected words and fragments of each group were read and compared with previous findings, particularly Tackman et al. (2020), Newman et al. (2008), and Mehl et al. (2006), to identify documented linguistic markers of personality and gender. Second, the same outputs were reviewed for gender-specific patterns not previously documented. Reading was done without a predefined coding scheme or counts; keyword searches within the selected fragments served only to locate examples. Across all groups, the selection yielded 327 unique fragments (180 female, 147 male), and the same fragment can be selected in more than one group. Excerpts reported in the Results and Tables were checked against the source fragments and lightly normalized (capitalization and spacing). Although selection was algorithm-driven, interpretation involves theoretical framing and researcher judgment; the examples therefore serve as illustrations.

Implementation Details

We fine-tuned the "bert-base-uncased" version of BERT with the Hugging Face Transformers library (Wolf et al., 2020) for PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019), tokenizing the fragments with the BERT tokenizer from the same library. The model was trained for three epochs with a batch size of 16, a learning rate of 4 × 10 -5 , a hidden dropout probability of 0.1, and an attention dropout probability of 0.2. After each epoch, we evaluated the model on the validation set and kept the checkpoint with the highest validation balanced accuracy.

Attribution scores were computed with the Transformers Interpret library 3 , which provides an integrated gradients implementation for transformers. This library applies a zero-embedding vector as the default reference baseline for integrated gradients, that is, a reference input in which all token embeddings are set to zero, representing the absence of any linguistic signal. This is a standard choice that satisfies the completeness property of integrated gradients, ensuring that attribution scores account for the full difference between the model's output on the actual text and on the empty baseline (Sundararajan et al., 2017); attribution scores are therefore interpretable relative to this baseline.

Experiments were run on a system with Intel Core I7, 32GB RAM, and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU using Python 3.11.1 with the following packages: transformers v4.40.1 (Wolf et al., 2020), PyTorch v2.3.0 (Paszke et al., 2019), transformersinterpret v0.10.0 (Pierse, 2021), scikit-learn v1.3.0 (Pedregosa et al., 2011), pandas v2.2.2 (McKinney, 2010), NumPy v1.23.5 (Harris et al., 2020), matplotlib v3.7.2 (Hunter, 2007), and seaborn v0.13.2 (Waskom, 2021). Statistical analyses and data visualization were conducted using R version 4.2.2 with readr v2.1.5 (Wickham, Hester, & Bryan, 2024), magrittr v2.0.3 (Bache & Wickham, 2022), dplyr v1.1.2 (Wickham et al., 2023), effectsize v0.8.9 (Ben-Shachar et al., 2020), patchwork v1.2.0 (Pedersen, 2024), ggplot2 v3.5.1 (Wickham, 2016), tidyr v1.3.1 (Wickham, Vaughan, & Girlich, 2024), and purrr v1.0.1 (Wickham & Henry, 2023).

Code and implementation details are available in our https://osf.io/5xz7w/?view_only=2a4174722b2e4a7aa38e83bafa031a37 (private during review, public upon publication).

Results

Initial Analysis of Gender Differences in Self-Reported Personality Scores

Initial analyses examined basic gender differences in personality traits using standardized scores. Cohen's d effect sizes revealed significant differences between males and females across all Big Five traits (see Figure 2). Females scored higher in Neuroticism (d = -0.45, [-0.53, -0.36]), Extraversion (d = -0.32, [-0.41, -0.24]), Agreeableness (d = -0.32, [-0.40, -0.23]), and Conscientiousness (d = -0.25, [-0.34, -0.17]). Males scored higher only in Openness to Experience, with a small effect (d = 0.17, [0.08, 0.25]). All effects were statistically significant based on 95% confidence intervals.

A logistic regression predicting gender from personality traits found all Big Five traits were significant predictors (p ≤ .001), with a balanced accuracy of 0.724. Neuroticism was the strongest predictor (OR = 2.11), followed by Extraversion (OR = 1.58) and Agreeableness (OR = 1.49). Conscientiousness showed a moderate effect (OR = 1.28), while Openness to Experience demonstrated an inverse relationship (OR = 0.83). The model significantly improved over the null model (residual deviance = 2672.9 vs null deviance = 3016.7) and showed acceptable fit (Hosmer-Lemeshow χ 2 (8) = 12.41, p = .134), explaining 19.2% of the variance (Nagelkerke R² ).

Results for Gender Only

General Gender Differences in Language Use

The BERT model achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.815 in classifying text segments by author gender. Two complementary analyses identify linguistic patterns that differ between males and females: a log-odds ratio analysis, whose z-scores are reported in Table 2, and word attribution scores from the classifier, presented in the explainability sections below.

Because "girlfriend" and "boyfriend" have gendered referents, gendered use of these terms is expected. A two-proportion z-test comparing "girlfriend" usage among males (234/898 = 26.1%) versus "boyfriend" usage among females (404/1342 = 30.1%), yielded a significant difference (z = -2.08, p = .037). Moreover, validation experiments using masked versions of these terms showed minimal impact on classification performance (balanced accuracy = 0.808 vs. 0.815, masked and original, respectively), suggesting that classification does not depend on them.

Log-odds ratio with IDP analysis identified 21 words with significant gender associations after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q < .05). Males showed stronger associations with activity terms (Newman et al., 2008; Park et al., 2016) ("play", "playing", "game", "music"), while females showed stronger associations with social-life terms (Newman et al., 2008; Park et al., 2016) ("sorority"), familial references (Newman et al., 2008) ("mom"), and the intensive adverb "really" (Park et al., 2016). Relationship terms ("girlfriend" for males, "boyfriend" for females) were also among these words, as expected given their gendered referents (see above). Complete results are presented in Table 2.

Explainability: Word Attribution Scores by Gender

Analysis of word attribution scores identified gender-specific language patterns. Using the maximum score summarization technique, we identified words with the strongest influence on gender classification (see Figure 4). For males, the highest attribution scores were for "girlfriend", "love", "roommate", "stream", and "band" (see Figure 3). Inspection of the underlying texts showed that the word itself presented small attribution scores for "love", "roommate", and "stream", and that their selection mainly reflects the surrounding essay, whereas "girlfriend" and "band" presented larger positive word-level scores. "Stream" in particular mostly comes from references to the writing task ("stream of consciousness") rather than from gendered content. The male list therefore points to romantic relationships and music more clearly than to social or leisure themes. (a) Female-associated linguistic patterns (b) Male-associated linguistic patterns For females, the highest attribution scores were for "boyfriend", "sorority", "cute", "girl", and "dance". These words were consistently highlighted in the texts, and they point to romantic relationships, social affiliations, and positive evaluations ("cute" was mostly used for boys and children), with "dance" referring to dance performance and events. "Girl" occurred both in self-reference and in references to other girls (see Figure 3).

Explainability: Whole Text Exploration by Gender

The following analysis is based on text segments selected through the attribution-score procedure described in Phase 3: Selection and Interpretation of Attribution Outputs. The examples come from a limited number of essays, were not systematically coded, and serve as illustrations only; the full attribution outputs are available on the https://osf.io/5xz7w/?view_only=2a4174722b2e4a7aa38e83bafa031a37.

In the high-scoring texts, we could not identify clear differences in writing style between male and female authors. Both genders disclosed emotions directly (females: "I feel really sad because I miss my family so bad"; males: "my biggest fear is never seeing my friends again") and both weighed options in practical terms (females: "which is more important? I guess more things will come up in the evenings than in the mornings"; males: "that would be very time consuming... I will have a lot to do besides"), and in both genders we found fragmented, topic-jumping texts as well as connected narratives. The differences we could identify concerned topical content, in line with the word-level results: for example, leisure activities such as dance for females ("I love to dance also, and I can't wait to try out for pom squad") and music for males ("I am listening to some audio adrenaline. they are a christian band I just downloaded"). Contrast constructions appeared in both genders, with somewhat different content: some male fragments used them for intellectual contrast ("although, in class you said…", "in general, not every woman"), whereas some female fragments used them around emotional and interpersonal concerns ("if only I could help him… but I know time is all he needs", "I am content… but I do miss"). Explicit sexual references appeared mainly in male texts ("thinking back to short, white hair and anonymous breasts", "she was drunk on our first date, she'd been with many other partners"), while the female relationship-focused fragments contained little explicit sexual language.

Results for Gender and Personality

Log-odds Ratio Analysis by Trait and Gender

This analysis asks which words distinguish men and women within the lowest (Q1) and highest (Q4) quartile of each trait. Each z-score compares men's and women's use of a word within the same quartile (negative values indicate male-associated words); it does not compare Q1 with Q4 within a gender. Table 3 lists the five most gender-distinctive words per group and gender regardless of significance (100 entries); 13 survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q < .05), 12 of them relationship terms with gendered referents: "girlfriend" (male-associated) in eight of the ten trait-quartile groups and "boyfriend" (female-associated) in four. The remaining word was the intensive adverb "really", femaleassociated in Neuroticism Q1 (z = 7.74); in Q4 it was also female-associated (z = 3.92) but did not survive correction. Because men contributed about half as much text in Q4 as in Q1 and the difference between quartiles was not tested, we do not take this contrast as evidence that the gender difference varies with trait level. All other listed words, including activity terms such as "playing" (among the top male-associated words in Q1 of four traits), did not survive correction and are reported as tentative.

For women, "boyfriend" had its highest z-scores in Agreeableness Q1 (z = 2.45), Extraversion Q1 (z = 2.33), and Neuroticism Q1 (z = 2.10). For men, "girlfriend" had its highest z-scores in Openness Q1 (z = -2.60), Neuroticism Q4 (z = -2.33), Conscientiousness Q4 (z = -2.25), and Agreeableness Q1 (z = -2.24). The size of the male-female contrast in these terms differed numerically between quartiles (e.g., in Openness, "girlfriend" z = -2.60 in Q1 vs -2.07 in Q4; "boyfriend" z = 2.07 in Q1 vs 1.62 in Q4), but we did not test whether these differences are reliable.

Explainability: Word Attribution Scores by Trait and Gender

Across the ten trait-quartile groups, the words with the highest attribution were largely the same in Q1 and Q4 and were dominated by gender-typical content. For females, "boyfriend" was among the two top words in every group, with consistently high word-level attribution scores (mean scores of about 0.7-0.9), followed by words such as "girl", "love", "cute", and "sorority". For males, the words were more heterogeneous and their wordlevel attribution scores were mostly lower (below 0.2 on average, with "girlfriend" as the exception), so their selection partly reflects the surrounding essay. Trait-related differences between quartiles were limited and are described below as tentative observations.

Openness to Experience.

At lower Openness levels (Q1), males' top words were leisure and activity terms ("music", "college", "football"), where "football" falls within the sports category that men used more in Newman et al. (2008), and females' were "sorority" and "boyfriend", words that point to social affiliation and relationships (Newman et al., 2008; Park et al., 2016). At higher Openness levels (Q4), males' top words were general evaluative and abstract terms ("great", "world", "good"), which presented small word-level scores and occurred in ordinary contexts (e.g., "such a great group", "the so called real world"), while females' were again relationship terms and positive evaluations (Park et al., 2016) ("boyfriend", "cute", "love"). Conscientiousness. At lower Conscientiousness levels (Q1), the male words ("though", "good", "first") were function words and general evaluatives with small wordlevel scores, so no content theme could be identified, while the female words were relational terms ("boyfriend", "girl", "someone"). At higher Conscientiousness levels (Q4), the male words were "girlfriend", "music", and "football" and the female words were "boyfriend", "cute", and "love". In neither quartile did the highlighted words refer to content related to the trait (e.g., planning or organization).

Extraversion. At lower Extraversion levels (Q1), males' top words were "music", "college", and "kind", the latter almost always in the hedge "kind of" (e.g., "i am kind of worried"), while females' were "boyfriend", "cute", "girl", and "hate", which mostly expressed dislike of tasks and things (e.g., reading, tests, weight) and not of people. At higher Extraversion levels (Q4), males' top words were "love", "girl", and "talk", mostly in contexts of romantic interest (e.g., "I'd like to talk to her", "I still love her"), while females' were "sorority" and "roommate", which refer to social organizations and shared living contexts (Park et al., 2016). In both genders the Q4 words refer somewhat more to social contact than the Q1 words, although the differences are small. Agreeableness. At lower Agreeableness levels (Q1), "girlfriend" was the male word with the most consistent word-level scores and appeared in contexts of current and former partners (e.g., "my ex-girlfriend from high school came in", "I wish I was at home with my girlfriend"), together with "music" and "college". Females' top words were relational terms ("boyfriend", "girl", "love") together with "hate", used in the same way as in Extraversion Q1. At higher Agreeableness levels (Q4), the male words ("girl", "talk", "love") appeared in contexts of attraction to or approaching a girl (e.g., "the girl I like will be there"), and "stream" mostly comes from references to the writing task. Females' words were "love", "miss", and "sister" (e.g., "right now I miss him. I feel love and sorrow"), which are affectionate terms, in line with the small female advantage in affiliative speech (Leaper & Ayres, 2007). We found no link between the contexts of the male words and Agreeableness itself.

Neuroticism. At lower Neuroticism levels (Q1), males' top words were "stream" (from the writing task), "girl" (with low and inconsistent word-level scores), and "music", while females' were relational terms ("boyfriend", "girl", "love"). At higher Neuroticism levels (Q4), males' words included "play", "college", "damn", and "though". "Damn" appeared in mild exclamations and complaints (e.g., "damn, I'm so freaking superficial", "this damn class") and swear words were used more by men in Newman et al. (2008), and "though" appeared in contexts such as "I miss her though". Females' words in Q4 were "boyfriend", "girl", "cute", and "love". Female words were similar in both quartiles, and male words varied more but with low word-level scores.

Explainability: Whole Text Exploration by Trait and Gender

We read the high-scoring essay fragments of each trait-quartile group against the general disposition described by each Big Five trait and the items of the Big Five Inventory. Across the ten groups, the texts were dominated by the gender-typical content already described and by everyday concerns of undergraduate students, which appeared in both quartiles of every trait. Differences between low (Q1) and high (Q4) trait levels were visible only in some groups and are described here as tentative impressions, each based on a small number of fragments; example excerpts are lightly normalized (capitalization and spacing).

For Openness, high-scoring men wrote more abstract and existential texts ("god is just santa clause for adults"; "we are all one consciousness functioning at different levels"), while we found no pattern in women.

For Conscientiousness, low-scoring men described laziness and distractibility ("I could quite possibly be the laziest person on this earth"; "I have always had a problem with being too easily distracted"), while high-scoring men more often referred to completing or preparing work ("I have just finished the rough draft of my rhetoric paper"; "maybe I will take a nap, except I have to study"); we found no such contrast in women, whose Q4 texts also included procrastination ("I was just looking for an excuse to put off my reading").

For Extraversion, low-scoring women more often described shyness or loneliness ("I have never really been one to mingle in a crowd"; "lately I have been feeling lonely, very lonely"), whereas we found no clear pattern in men.

For Agreeableness, annoyance and criticism of others appeared in both quartiles of both genders (e.g., "it annoys me to no extent when people don't keep up with it", female Q4), so we could not identify differences by trait level.

For Neuroticism, texts of both genders in Q1 often paired distress with positive reappraisal ("besides the occasional loneliness, I am very happy with my new life here at college", male; "other than feeling really tired and lazy, I am also feeling happy", female), whereas Q4 texts more often stated worry or irritation without such reappraisal ("I've always had so much to do that when I don't, I can't relax and I get really anxious", female; "if we're friends then why do I find myself mad at her all the time", male). Distress was also present in Q1 texts.

Verbatim excerpts for each impression are given in Table 4, and Table 5 summarizes the word-level and whole-text results by trait and quartile.

Discussion

This study investigated how gender and personality interact in natural language expression using XAI techniques. Our findings suggest that (1) the model and the attribution outputs capture clear gender-typical content, consistent with prior work on gender differences in language; (2) trait-specific differences within each gender could be identified only tentatively, with no clear pattern for Agreeableness; and (3) attribution-based explainability can surface such patterns for qualitative inspection, although it does not by itself establish them.

General Discussion

Gender-Personality Interactions in Language

The qualitative observations discussed below come from attribution-selected texts (see Phase 3: Selection and Interpretation of Attribution Outputs); because the final reading involves researcher judgment and the examples were neither systematically coded nor statistically tested, we present them as illustrative, candidate patterns rather than established effects.

Gender-Typical Content.

The word attribution analysis shows clear genderspecific patterns that are consistent with previous findings (Mehl et al., 2006; Park et al., 2016). The highest-attribution words mainly reflect what men and women write about rather than how they write it. Both lists combine relationship terms, which reflect gendered referents ("girlfriend" for males, "boyfriend" for females), with terms for social and leisure settings ("roommate" and "band" for males, "sorority" and "dance" for females), and they differ more in the particular settings mentioned than in kind; positive evaluation ("cute") also appears among the female words.

Trait-Level Patterns Within Each Gender.

While prior research has identified broad distinctions in male and female language (Newman et al., 2008; Tackman et al., 2020), our trait-level analyses suggest that these distinctions vary somewhat within each gender. The whole-text reading suggested patterns that fit the content of the traits (Table 4): reappraisal of distress at low Neuroticism in both genders, with irritation among men and worry among women at high Neuroticism; laziness versus work completion among men at the two ends of Conscientiousness; shyness among low-Extraversion women; and abstract reflections among high-Openness men. These patterns are in line with earlier evidence that personality is expressed in language (Mehl et al., 2006; Tackman et al., 2020). Across trait levels, however, the attribution outputs were dominated by the same gender-typical content found in the gender-only analysis, so whether and how trait level modulates gendered language remains open and would require larger samples and designs built for the interaction.

Comparison With Earlier Findings. Some of our observations can be compared with earlier work, although our written, stream-of-consciousness data are a reasonable but not equivalent basis for comparison with the spoken-language studies of Mehl et al. (2006) and Tackman et al. (2020). Newman et al. (2008) found a small gender difference in the use of discrepancy words (e.g., "should", "would", "could"), with women using them slightly more than men (d = 0.07). In the attribution-selected fragments we read, contrast constructions appeared in both genders with somewhat different content (see Results). These examples cannot show that the small aggregate difference reflects different communicative functions, but they suggest that attribution-based reading can complement word counts.

In contrast, Newman et al. (2008) reported that men and women were "indistinguishable in their references to sexuality" (p. 229). In the fragments we read, explicit sexual references appeared mainly in male texts (see Results), which is not consistent with that finding. It may partly reflect our data collection: stream-of-consciousness essays written in private and anonymously may have reduced self-censorship compared with the contexts analyzed by Newman et al. (2008). It is also in line with Tackman et al. (2020), who reported gender-specific personality correlates of sexual language (men high in Extraversion used more sexual words).

Anger and swearing were less informative. Tackman et al. (2020) reported that the tendency of agreeable individuals to avoid anger and swear words appeared only among women, and Newman et al. (2008) found that men used more swear words overall (d = -0.22) but did not differ from women in anger words. In our data, profanity (e.g., "asshole") appeared in both male and female fragments, and the Agreeableness cells of Table 4 show no clear gender-specific pattern, so we cannot corroborate the gender-specific agreeableness result.

For low Extraversion, Mehl et al. (2006) and Tackman et al. (2020) reported that less extraverted individuals spend more time alone and talk less. In our whole-text reading, women at low Extraversion wrote about shyness and loneliness, which is consistent with low Extraversion, whereas we found no clear pattern among men (Table 4).

Relationship Terms Across Trait Groups.

The male-female contrast in relationship terms differed numerically across trait groups (see Results). These differences between quartiles were not tested, and only 13 of the 100 words listed in Table 3 survived correction, 12 of them relationship terms. We do not interpret these differences psychologically; whether a gendered vocabulary varies in strength across trait groups would need to be tested with matched subgroup sizes. Similarly, the intensive adverb "really", which women used more than men in the whole sample, in line with Park et al. (2016), remained significant among participants low in Neuroticism but not among those high in it. Whether the gender difference in intensive adverbs weakens at high Neuroticism is a hypothesis for confirmatory work with a direct test of the interaction.

Overall Pattern. These comparisons are mixed: the gender-typical content and the low-Extraversion pattern are consistent with earlier research (Mehl et al., 2006; Tackman et al., 2020), whereas the sexual-language and Agreeableness results are not. The classifier's balanced accuracy (0.815) is well above chance but far from perfect, so these differences should be read as tendencies in the text fragments rather than a clean separation between men's and women's writing.

Methodological Contributions and Considerations

What Attribution Adds. Our use of XAI techniques, in particular BERT with integrated gradients, shows which words drive the classifier's predictions for each gender and trait group. This method identifies specific words and phrases that influence model predictions, providing insight into how BERT makes decisions about gender by attributing importance to specific linguistic features (Sundararajan et al., 2017).

A bottom-up analysis can detect variables and interactions that were not specified in advance (Boyd & Markowitz, 2024). Our results are consistent with the ability of XAI to surface patterns that align with theoretical frameworks, but they do not by themselves validate the method.

Compared with TF-IDF and logistic regression, the main difference is contextual sensitivity. Unlike bag-of-words methods that treat each word as an isolated unit with fixed importance regardless of surrounding text, BERT generates contextualized embeddings where the same word receives different representations depending on its linguistic environment (Devlin et al., 2019). For instance, as reported in the Results, for several male words (e.g., "stream", "roommate", "love") the word itself received attribution near zero and its selection mainly reflected the surrounding essay, a distinction that a fixed perword weight in bag-of-words approaches cannot capture. More broadly, the attribution outputs suggest that the model's decisions are not limited to a few gendered words, since the attribution-selected texts also contain topical and emotional content.

Classification performance should be read with the same caution. A balanced accuracy of 0.815 shows that the model detects gender-related signal in the essays, but not what that signal consists of. Attribution outputs make it possible to check whether the words driving the predictions are consistent with prior theory. In our data they partly are: the highest-attribution words reflect relationship, social, and leisure content, whereas trait-specific differences within each gender were modest and tentative. High accuracy is therefore a reason to inspect the model, not evidence that it captures theoretically meaningful differences, and attribution methods are what make that inspection possible.

The Data Source. The stream-of-consciousness format may also capture less self-censored, more spontaneous expression than traditional assessment methods (e.g., questionnaires). Unlike self-reports, which are vulnerable to social desirability bias, acquiescence, and self-deception (Paulhus & Vazire, 2007), naturalistic language analysis might be less exposed to these biases, as it examines spontaneous verbal expression rather than deliberate self-evaluation.

Our methodological framework (Saeteros et al., 2025) combines naturalistic language data with XAI techniques, and their contributions should be kept apart. The freedom from self-report biases stems from the data source itself, not from the model; what XAI adds is the ability to inspect which words and texts drive the model's predictions for each gender and trait group. The patterns reported here suggest the potential of this combination to describe fine-grained differences that complement existing measurement methods, and offer a possible template for interpreting complex psychological constructs through theoretically grounded language analysis (Grahek et al., 2021).

Relation to Dictionary-Based Methods.

Our transformer-based approach with XAI is intended to complement dictionary-based methods. Methods like LIWC remain useful for hypothesis-driven research where theoretical expectations are clear, offering transparency and replicability, and questionnaires capture aspects of personality expression, such as conscious self-concepts, that behavioral data cannot access. Contextual embeddings combined with integrated gradients add the possibility of examining context-dependent patterns in language.

Gender-Identifying Terms and Lexical Cues.

Another methodological consideration is the role of gender-identifying terms such as "boyfriend/girlfriend", which might be considered obvious lexical cues. We retained them for two reasons. First, previous work on gender-personality interactions in language, including Tackman et al. (2020), treats relationship terms as meaningful indicators of linguistic expression. Second, they appear in only a minority of essays, and masking them left classification performance essentially unchanged (see Results), so the classifier does not depend on them alone.

Moreover, BERT's architecture encode more than lexical choices: as Rogers et al. (2020) document, BERT's multiple layers encode morphological, syntactic, and semantic information through contextualized embeddings. Integrated gradients allows us to inspect which words drive classification decisions. In our outputs, the highest-attribution words were mostly content words (e.g., relationship terms, social and leisure settings), with a few function words (e.g., "though", "someone") among the trait-level words. This differs in emphasis from LIWC-based approaches, which have highlighted function words, sentence length, and other syntactic categories (Newman et al., 2008; Pennebaker et al., 2003; Tackman et al., 2020); because we did not compare predictive power across linguistic levels, we cannot conclude that semantic content is more informative than these categories.

Bias and Demographic Membership.

We urge caution when interpreting our findings, because several questions arise when working with language and ML methods (Van Der Wal et al., 2024). First, language carries substantial information about the speaker, their self-identification, and membership in socio-demographic groups (Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021). Second, language conveys information about the society the speaker inhabits (Caliskan et al., 2017).

With this in mind, it is possible that the results discussed above carry biases present in the data used for our analyses. By bias, in a strictly probabilistic sense, we refer to a deviation from the expectation we should have for something before we see any further evidence (Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021). In this sample of undergraduate students from the early 2000s, for instance, men are more likely to write "girlfriend" and women "boyfriend" than the reverse. An alternative explanation for our results could therefore be that we are detecting membership in a socio-demographic group at a certain point in time rather than meaningful linguistic differences between genders. However, two observations suggest that the model captures signal beyond demographic markers: masking these terms left performance essentially unchanged, and the attribution outputs point to diverse features.

Implications & Applications

Our findings point to three implications, which we present as directions rather than conclusions.

First, for the study of gender and personality in language, the attribution outputs show that a gender classifier relies heavily on gender-typical content, particularly relationship terms. The trait-specific patterns that emerged within each gender (Table 4) can be stated as testable gender × trait interactions: (a) at high Neuroticism, negative affect is expressed more as irritation or anger by men and more as worry or anxiety by women, in line with the female-specific association between Neuroticism and sadness words reported by Tackman et al. (2020); (b) Conscientiousness is more strongly associated with references to completing or avoiding work among men than among women; (c) low Extraversion is more strongly associated with references to shyness and loneliness among women than among men; and (d) Openness is more strongly associated with abstract and existential content among men than among women. An association between Openness and abstract concepts has been reported in the same corpus without separating by gender (Saeteros et al., 2025), so only the gender-specific part of this prediction is new. Because these hypotheses were derived from the present data, they should be tested in independent corpora.

Second, for language-based personality assessment, Tackman et al. (2020) found genderspecific associations between personality and language, which suggests that models should not assume the same mapping for men and women. Our classifier predicted gender, not personality, and masking the relationship terms barely changed its accuracy; whether gendered content affects language-based personality models would need to be tested directly.

Third, attribution-guided reading can surface candidate patterns that broader statistical approaches might miss (Mõttus, 2022), complementing traditional methods that have identified robust patterns (Soto, 2019). The same approach could be applied to other longstanding questions in personality and individual differences, such as the relation between personality and culture (Allik et al., 2023).

Limitations & Future Directions

Several limitations should be noted. The most significant is that our sample consists of predominantly Western undergraduate students writing stream-of-consciousness essays in an academic setting, which may have shaped language use and may limit generalization to other age groups, populations and cultural contexts (Costa et al., 2001). Language also varies across age groups (Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021), so the patterns identified here may not hold elsewhere.

An important limitation concerns the challenge of separating linguistic style from topical content in stream-of-consciousness essays. Because the instruction did not specify a topic, participants wrote about diverse subjects, creating potential confounds between what people discuss and how they express themselves (e.g., "girlfriend/boyfriend" may indicate relationship focus rather than linguistic style). Although the masking check and the diversity of attributed features suggest that the patterns are not limited to such content, this cannot be conclusively established without additional datasets collected with different methods.

In addition, the trait groups were defined from global self-report scores, which may partly reflect self-image, identity and gender norms (Buck et al., 2026). Males and females with similar scores may therefore not be equivalent in their underlying trait levels, and our trait groups should be read as groups defined by questionnaire scores. The Big Five items were administered with simplified wording, which may limit comparability with standard BFI scores.

A further limitation concerns the review of the extensive attribution outputs generated by integrated gradients, which produce attribution scores for every word in every text, a volume too large to analyze comprehensively by hand. We therefore used attribution scores to select the words and texts to read (see Phase 3: Selection and Interpretation of Attribution Outputs), so that selection is driven by the model rather than by the researchers. The final step of reading and choosing examples nevertheless involves researcher judgment, and our synthesis is illustrative rather than exhaustive. The reading was done by a single reader without an inter-rater check, the same fragment can be selected in several groups, some high-attribution texts were hard to interpret, and the trait-quartile groups are small, so a few essays can dominate a group.

Future research should pursue three directions. First, the candidate patterns reported here should be tested for replication across larger samples, age groups, cultures and communication contexts, for instance by applying these XAI techniques to other spontaneous language datasets, such as those used by Tackman et al. (2020) or the Reddit-based PAN-DORA corpus (Gjurković et al., 2021). This is also relevant because recent studies on LLMs, such as Peters and Matz (2024), highlight the potential for demographic biases in psychological profiling, with more accurate personality inferences observed for women compared to men. Second, controlled designs that hold content constant across participants (e.g., standardized writing prompts) or systematically vary topic assignment would help separate linguistic style from content. Third, the judgment-based last step of our procedure could be made more objective, for instance by using embedding-based similarity (e.g., cosine similarity between attribution-selected fragments) to group and retrieve texts, and computational methods for synthesizing attribution outputs at scale would make such analyses more comprehensive and reproducible.

Conclusion

Using integrated gradients on a BERT gender classifier, we found that the attribution outputs capture clear gender-typical content, mainly relationship terms and social and leisure settings, in line with prior work. Within each gender, a few trait-specific patterns emerged, which we state as four testable gender × trait interactions (see Implications) for larger samples and more automated analysis techniques. Attribution-guided reading thus offers a way to generate hypotheses about how gender and personality are expressed in language, which designs built for the gender-trait interaction can then evaluate.

Open Data

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all data inclusion/exclusion criteria, whether inclusion/exclusion criteria were established prior to data analysis, all measures in the study, and all analyses including all tested models. If we use inferential tests, we report exact p values, effect sizes, and 95% confidence or credible intervals.

Open Data: The Essays dataset was obtained by email from its original author (Pennebaker & King, 1999) and is not redistributed by us; it can be requested from the original author. The attribution outputs, word-level results and tables derived from it are available in the https://osf.io/5xz7w/?view_only=2a4174722b2e4a7aa38e83bafa031a37 which is private (view-only link) during review and will be made public upon publication.

Open Materials: The materials needed to reproduce the reported methodology, including the figures and tables, are available in the same OSF repository under the same access conditions.

Preregistration of Studies and Analysis Plans: This study was not preregistered. Open Analytic Code: The scripts and code needed to reproduce all of the reported results are available in the same OSF repository under the same access conditions.
